purpose: Edaravone is used to treat ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig's disease. It helps slow down the decline in physical function that ALS causes. It does not cure ALS, but it may help patients maintain their abilities a little longer.
how_it_works: ALS causes harmful particles called free radicals to build up in your nerve cells and damage them. Edaravone works like a sponge by soaking up and neutralizing those harmful free radicals. This helps protect your nerve cells from further damage and may slow the progression of the disease.
common_side_effects: Bruising, walking difficulties, headache, and skin sores at the IV site. You might also notice swelling, or feel generally unwell during or after treatment. Some patients experience a rash or itching.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you are allergic to edaravone or sodium bisulfite, as a serious allergic reaction is possible. If you have asthma, you may be at higher risk for a reaction. The IV form contains sulfite, which can cause reactions in sensitive people. Let your healthcare team know right away if you notice hives, trouble breathing, or swelling of the face or throat during infusion.
typical_dosing: The treatment is given in cycles. The first cycle involves getting an infusion every day for 14 days. After that, each cycle is 14 days on, followed by 14 days off. Your doctor or infusion center will schedule and manage your treatments. An oral liquid form (Radicava ORS) is also available and is taken by mouth once daily following the same cycle schedule.
